people.name: Bhagat Singh Thind
body: In 1917, when the United States entered World War I, a young Sikh man from Punjab enlisted in the U.S. Army. He trained at Camp Lewis in Washington wearing his turban, a requirement of his faith. The National Park Service calls him the first turbaned soldier in the American military. He was honorably discharged in 1918. What he wanted next was citizenship in the country he had served.

Bhagat Singh Thind was born in 1892 in Amritsar district, Punjab, in British-ruled India. He came to Seattle in 1913, one of thousands of Indian men who arrived in the Pacific Northwest in those years. He studied religion and literature at the University of California, Berkeley, and spent summers working in lumber mills in Astoria, Oregon. There he joined the Ghadar Party, a movement working to end British colonial rule in India.

At the time, federal law allowed only "free white persons" and people of African descent to naturalize. Thind's first grant of citizenship was reversed after the Bureau of Naturalization objected. In November 1920 an Oregon court granted it again, citing his military service, and the government appealed. In February 1923 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously in United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind that people from India were not "white" in the common meaning of the word, so they could not become citizens. The Court used that reasoning even though it accepted that Indians were classified as "Caucasian" in the science of the day.

The ruling hurt people right away. Indian Americans who had already naturalized had their citizenship taken away. In California, where non-citizens could not own land, many lost their farms. Thind finally became a citizen in the mid-1930s, after Congress passed a 1935 law opening citizenship to World War I veterans. He spent the rest of his life writing and lecturing across the country on spirituality and Sikh thought. He died in Los Angeles in 1967.
keyFacts: 1892: Born in Amritsar district, Punjab.
1913: Arrived in Seattle.
1917–1918: Served in the U.S. Army and was honorably discharged.
1923: The Supreme Court ruled against him in United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind.
Mid-1930s: Became a citizen under a 1935 law for veterans. The National Park Service gives 1935; the Princeton Undergraduate Law Journal gives 1936.
1967: Died in Los Angeles.
people.connectToWork: Thind's status changed with a court's reading of one word. Which of your eligibility rules depend on a category someone else defined, and how would you check what that category does to the person in front of you?

people.name: Dalip Singh Saund
body: In 1956, voters in California's Imperial Valley, a desert farming region on the Mexican border, elected a Sikh farmer with a Ph.D. in mathematics to the U.S. House of Representatives. Dalip Singh Saund became the first Indian American and the first person of any Asian descent elected to Congress. Only seven years earlier, the law had not let him become a citizen at all.

Saund was born in 1899 in Punjab, then under British rule. He came to the United States in 1920 to study at the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned a master's degree and a Ph.D. in mathematics. Because he could not naturalize, he could not get a teaching job, so he farmed in the Imperial Valley for about two decades. California's laws kept non-citizen Asians from owning land.

Saund did not accept that exclusion. He helped campaign against the citizenship ban, and that work contributed to the 1946 Luce-Celler Act, which President Truman signed. The act allowed people from India and the Philippines to naturalize. Saund became a citizen in 1949. In 1950 he won election as a local justice of the peace.

In Congress, Saund was a Democrat who spoke for Southern California farmers and for immigrants' rights. On the House Foreign Affairs Committee he worked to strengthen ties between the U.S. and India. He took office in January 1957 and won reelection twice. In 1962, while running for a fourth term, he had a severe stroke. He won the primary but lost the general election. He died in 1973.
keyFacts: 1899: Born in Punjab, British India.
1920: Enrolled at the University of California, Berkeley, where he later earned a Ph.D. in mathematics.
1946: The Luce-Celler Act opened naturalization to Indians. PBS credits his campaign as part of what led to it.
1949: Became a U.S. citizen.
1956: Elected to the U.S. House from California's Imperial Valley.
1962: Lost his seat after a stroke. He died in 1973.
people.connectToWork: Saund could not get a teaching job until the law changed, whatever his degree said. Where might a rule in your area still be keeping out people who already have the qualifications?

people.name: Kalpana Chawla
body: In November 1997, the Space Shuttle Columbia lifted off on mission STS-87. One of its mission specialists, the prime operator of the shuttle's robotic arm, was Kalpana Chawla. With that flight she became the first woman born in India to travel to space.

Chawla was born in Karnal, India. She earned an engineering degree at Punjab Engineering College in 1982 and moved to the United States for graduate school. She earned two master's degrees at the University of Texas at Arlington (1984 and 1986) and a doctorate at the University of Colorado Boulder in 1988. After that she did research on airflow around aircraft for NASA projects and worked in private industry in California. She became a U.S. citizen in 1990.

NASA turned down her first astronaut application. She was accepted on her second try and began training in March 1995. On the 1997 mission she deployed the Spartan satellite. It malfunctioned, and crewmates had to recapture it on a spacewalk.

In January 2003 she launched again on Columbia, mission STS-107, a research flight on which she served as flight engineer and ran experiments on how flames behave. On February 1, 2003, the shuttle broke apart over Texas as it came back through the atmosphere, and all seven astronauts died. Investigators traced the disaster to foam that broke off and damaged the wing during launch.
keyFacts: 1962: Born in Karnal, India. Spacefacts gives March 17, 1962, and says a 1961 date was given to school authorities so she could start school early.
1982: Earned an engineering degree from Punjab Engineering College.
1988: Earned a Ph.D. in aerospace engineering from the University of Colorado Boulder.
1990: Became a U.S. citizen.
1997: Flew on STS-87 aboard Columbia.
2003: Died in the Columbia disaster on February 1.
people.connectToWork: NASA said no the first time, and Chawla applied again. When someone in your service is turned down, what do they learn about whether and how to try again?

people.name: Satveer Chaudhary
body: In the November 1996 election, voters in the northern suburbs of the Twin Cities sent a 27-year-old to the Minnesota House of Representatives. Satveer Chaudhary was born in Minneapolis to Indian immigrant parents. MNopedia identifies him as the first Asian American member of the Minnesota Legislature and the fourth person with Asian Indian ancestry elected to a state legislature in the United States.

Chaudhary's career tracks the growth of Minnesota's Indian community after 1965. That year, the Immigration and Nationality Act ended the national-origin quotas that had kept most Indians out. Professionals, students and families then began settling in the Twin Cities. Chaudhary was born in 1969 and grew up as one of that generation's children. He graduated from Columbia Heights High School and earned a degree in political science from St. Olaf College in 1991. He also studied at Oxford and earned his law degree from the University of Minnesota in 1995.

He served two terms in the House, starting in 1997, and moved to the Minnesota Senate in 2001. He represented suburban districts north of Minneapolis until January 2011. As a DFL senator he served as majority whip from 2003 to 2006. He also chaired the Senate's Environment and Natural Resources Committee, which oversees hunting, fishing, and the state's lakes and lands. In 2010 he lost the primary to Barb Goodwin, and his Senate service ended in January 2011.
keyFacts: 1969: Born in Minneapolis.
1991: Earned a B.A. from St. Olaf College.
1995: Earned a J.D. from the University of Minnesota Law School.
1996: Elected to the Minnesota House, serving from 1997 to 2000.
2001–2010: Served in the Minnesota Senate and chaired its Environment and Natural Resources Committee.
people.connectToWork: Chaudhary's committee work was on hunting, fishing and lakes. When you look for someone to speak on an issue, do you only ask people from a community about matters labeled as that community's concerns?

people.name: Ranee Ramaswamy
body: In 1990 an Indian-born dancer in Minneapolis met the Minnesota poet Robert Bly. The meeting led to Mirabai Versions (1991), a production that combined Bly's English versions of poems by the 16th-century Indian poet-saint Mirabai with music and Bharatanatyam dance. Its premiere encouraged Ranee Ramaswamy to found a company. In 1992 she started Ragamala in Minneapolis, which MNopedia calls a leading dance ensemble of the Indian diaspora in the United States.

Ramaswamy grew up in Chennai (formerly Madras) and trained in Bharatanatyam from age nine to nineteen. Bharatanatyam is a classical dance form from Tamil Nadu with roots in temple traditions. It tells stories from Hindu literature through precise footwork, gesture and facial expression. In 1978 she moved to Minneapolis with her husband and young daughter Aparna. From 1983 to 1990 she traveled back to India every year to study with the dancer Alarmél Valli.

MNopedia credits her and sitarist David Whetstone as co-founders. Whetstone left in 1996. Ragamala grew into a family-led company. Aparna Ramaswamy became co-artistic director in 2002, and her sister Ashwini joined as choreographic associate in 2016. As of October 2026 the company lists Aparna as executive artistic director and Ranee as co-artistic director. The company has created works such as Sacred Earth (2011), Song of the Jasmine (2014) and Written in Water, which was performed at Jacob's Pillow in 2018. Ragamala teaches students in the Twin Cities and tours nationally and abroad.

Ranee Ramaswamy received the McKnight Distinguished Artist Award in 2011, a Doris Duke Performing Artist Award in 2014, and a Guggenheim Fellowship in choreography in 2018, the same year Aparna received one.
keyFacts: 1978: Moved to Minneapolis.
1991: Mirabai Versions premiered, made with Robert Bly.
1992: Founded Ragamala in Minneapolis with David Whetstone.
2011: Received the McKnight Distinguished Artist Award.
2014: Received a Doris Duke Performing Artist Award.
2018: Received a Guggenheim Fellowship in choreography.
people.connectToWork: Ragamala's work is both a Minnesota art form and a lineage from India. How would you find out what a program participant wants to keep, share or change, rather than assuming what their tradition means to them?

people.name: Aparna Ramaswamy
body: Aparna Ramaswamy came to Minneapolis as a small child in 1978, when her mother, Ranee Ramaswamy, moved here with the family. She went on to study with the same teacher her mother did, the Bharatanatyam dancer Alarmél Valli, and Ragamala's site calls her a life-long disciple.

She became co-artistic director of Ragamala in 2002. As of October 2026 the company lists her as executive artistic director, choreographer and principal dancer. In 2018 she and her mother both received Guggenheim Fellowships.
keyFacts: 1978: Came to Minneapolis as a young child.
2002: Became co-artistic director of Ragamala.
2018: Received a Guggenheim Fellowship.
people.connectToWork: How do you plan for the handover when an organization you rely on moves from its founder to the next generation?

people.name: Raghavan Iyer
body: Raghavan Iyer grew up in Mumbai and came to the United States as a young man to study hospitality. By his own account, he was at first embarrassed by the food of his childhood. After he settled in Minnesota, the lack of Indian food nearby pushed him to cook his favorite dishes himself. He then pitched an idea to Minnesota-based General Mills. The result was Betty Crocker's Indian Home Cooking (2001), which brought Indian cooking into the most mainstream of American kitchen brands.

From his Minneapolis base, Iyer became one of the best-known teachers of Indian cooking in the country. He wrote seven books, including The Turmeric Trail (a 2003 James Beard Award finalist for best international cookbook), 660 Curries (2008), and Smashed, Mashed, Boiled, and Baked—and Fried, Too! (2016). He consulted for restaurants, taught workshops, led food tours to India, created a frozen Indian meal line for Minneapolis-based Target, and trained thousands of professional cooks. The International Association of Culinary Professionals named him Cooking Teacher of the Year in 2004.

He kept writing through cancer treatment. His last book, On the Curry Trail: Chasing the Flavor That Seduced the World, came out in February 2023. It traces how curry traveled around the world. He died on March 31, 2023, in San Francisco, at age 61.
keyFacts: 1961: Born, and grew up in Mumbai.
2001: Published Betty Crocker's Indian Home Cooking.
2003: The Turmeric Trail was a James Beard Award finalist.
2004: Named Cooking Teacher of the Year by the International Association of Culinary Professionals.
2008: Published 660 Curries.
2023: Published On the Curry Trail in February and died in San Francisco on March 31.
people.connectToWork: Iyer's books treated Indian food as many regional cuisines. Where does your program use one word, such as Indian, for what are really several languages, diets or traditions?

people.name: Neel Kashkari
body: In October 2008, during the financial crisis, a 35-year-old Treasury official named Neel Kashkari set up and led the Office of Financial Stability, which ran the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), the federal rescue of the banking system. He served under both President George W. Bush and President Barack Obama.

Kashkari was born on July 30, 1973, in Akron, Ohio, and MNopedia describes him as a second-generation Indian American. He earned bachelor's and master's degrees in mechanical engineering at the University of Illinois and worked as an aerospace engineer at TRW. He then earned an MBA from the Wharton School and became a vice president at Goldman Sachs in San Francisco. In 2006 he joined the Treasury Department as a senior adviser to Secretary Henry Paulson.

After Treasury he worked as a managing director at the investment firm PIMCO. He left in 2013 and ran for governor of California in 2014 but did not win. On January 1, 2016, he became the 13th president and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis. The bank serves the Ninth District, which covers Minnesota, Montana, the Dakotas, northwestern Wisconsin and Michigan's Upper Peninsula. In that role he helps set national monetary policy on the Federal Open Market Committee. As of October 2026 he remains the bank's president.
He followed Narayana Kocherlakota, another Indian American, as the bank's president. MNopedia notes both men as second-generation Indian Americans who led the Minneapolis Fed.
keyFacts: 1973: Born in Akron, Ohio.
2006–2009: Served at the U.S. Treasury as senior adviser and then assistant secretary.
2008–2009: Led the Office of Financial Stability and TARP.
2014: Ran for governor of California.
2016: Became the 13th president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis on January 1.
people.connectToWork: Interest rate decisions reach Minnesota households through jobs and loans. When money gets tighter for the people you serve, how would you tell a change in the economy apart from a change in the person?

people.name: Narayana Kocherlakota
body: Before Neel Kashkari, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis was another economist whom MNopedia describes as a second-generation Indian American. Narayana Kocherlakota led the bank from 2009 to 2015 and served on the Federal Open Market Committee, which sets national monetary policy.

He earned a Ph.D. in economics from the University of Chicago in 1987 and taught at Stanford, Northwestern, the University of Iowa and the University of Minnesota. As of October 2026 the University of Rochester's Simon Business School lists him as Louise and Henry Epstein Professor of Business Administration and senior associate dean of faculty and research.
keyFacts: 1987: Earned a Ph.D. in economics from the University of Chicago.
2009–2015: President and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.
people.connectToWork: Two people from one background in a row can lead an institution without any one of them speaking for a group. How do you avoid treating a leader's background as a statement about what that leader thinks?

people.name: Sumita Mitra
body: If you have had a tooth-colored filling in the past twenty years, it may have come from a 3M lab in Minnesota, from work led by Sumita Mitra. In the late 1990s she and her team developed the first dental filling material made with nanoparticles. It went on the market in 2002 as Filtek Supreme Universal Restorative. Its mix of tiny particles and particle clusters made fillings strong and wear-resistant, and they kept their polish like a natural tooth.

Mitra was born in India in 1949. She studied chemistry at Presidency College and earned a master's in organic chemistry at the University of Calcutta in 1972. She came to the United States and earned a doctorate in organic and polymer chemistry at the University of Michigan in 1977. In 1978 she joined 3M in the Twin Cities as a senior chemist. In 1983 she moved to the group that became 3M Oral Care. She worked there for more than 30 years until she retired in 2010.

The National Inventors Hall of Fame says she holds more than 100 U.S. patents, and that her Filtek materials have been used in more than a billion restorations worldwide. She was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2018. In 2021 she was elected to the National Academy of Engineering and won the European Inventor Award. MNopedia also notes that she and her husband, Sam Mitra, both 3M research scientists, won the highest technical awards their company offers.
keyFacts: 1949: Born in India.
1977: Earned a Ph.D. from the University of Michigan.
1978: Joined 3M.
2002: Filtek Supreme nanocomposite launched.
2018: Inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame.
2021: Elected to the National Academy of Engineering and won the European Inventor Award.
people.connectToWork: A filling most people never think about came from a Minnesota lab led by an immigrant chemist. Whose everyday contributions does your team overlook when it talks about the people it serves?

people.name: Fred de Sam Lazaro
body: Since 1985, viewers of the PBS NewsHour have watched reports from a correspondent based in St. Paul, who had reported from 68 countries by 2018. Many were stories about health, poverty and development that big newsrooms often skip. That reporter is Fred de Sam Lazaro. He has built his career on the idea that some of the world's most important stories are "under-told."

De Sam Lazaro was born in Bangalore, India, in 1956, the youngest of twelve children. After his father died, he and his mother joined his sister in San Francisco in 1975. He went to the College of Marin, then moved to Duluth, where he graduated from the College of St. Scholastica in 1981 with a degree in media arts. An internship at Minnesota Public Radio in Duluth turned into a full-time job.

In 1985 St. Paul's public TV station, KTCA (now TPT), hired him as a field reporter for Almanac. Two months later the MacNeil/Lehrer program, the predecessor of today's PBS NewsHour, hired him as a regional correspondent. He has worked for the program ever since and has also reported for Religion & Ethics NewsWeekly.

In 2006 he founded the Under-Told Stories Project at Saint John's University in Collegeville. It moved to Saint Mary's University of Minnesota in 2011, and since January 2016 it has been based at the University of St. Thomas in St. Paul. The project produces global reporting and uses it to teach students about urgent world issues. As of October 2026, PBS News is still running his reports.
keyFacts: 1956: Born in Bangalore, India.
1981: Graduated from the College of St. Scholastica in Duluth.
1985: Hired by KTCA and then by the MacNeil/Lehrer program on PBS.
2006: Founded the Under-Told Stories Project at Saint John's University.
2016: The project moved to the University of St. Thomas.
people.connectToWork: Whose stories does your program never hear about because no one in the room thought to ask? How could you find one this month?

people.name: Srilata (Sri) Zaheer
body: In March 2012, the University of Minnesota named a long-time faculty member to lead its business school. Srilata "Sri" Zaheer became the 12th dean of the Carlson School of Management on March 8, 2012, and served until July 2, 2023. She had taught at the school for more than 20 years.

Zaheer earned a physics degree at Madras University in 1973, a postgraduate business degree at the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad in 1975, and a Ph.D. in international management at MIT in 1992. She joined the Carlson School faculty in 1991. Her research looked at the risks multinational companies face when they operate abroad, and at how technology shapes where and how global businesses organize. She was named a Fellow of the Academy of International Business in 2007. She also holds the Elmer L. Andersen chair in global corporate social responsibility, named for a former Minnesota governor.

During her deanship she launched a Military Veterans Initiative and oversaw new degrees in business analytics, supply chain management and finance, partnerships with Tsinghua and Tongji universities in China, and online programs. She also served as chair of the board of directors of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, and as of October 2026 the Carlson School lists her as professor and dean emerita.

Before becoming dean she was associate dean of faculty and research, and then interim dean. An international search ended with her appointment. She was also a consulting editor of the Journal of International Business Studies and a founding member of the International Academic Council of the Indian School of Business.
keyFacts: 1991: Joined the Carlson School faculty.
2007: Named a Fellow of the Academy of International Business.
2012: Became 12th dean of the Carlson School on March 8.
2020: Chair of the Minneapolis Fed board of directors.
2023: Stepped down as dean on July 2.
people.connectToWork: Who in your organization came as a student or a newcomer and now leads? What did it take, and what would make that path shorter for the next person?

people.name: Hira Singh
people.dates: Enrolled at the University of Minnesota in 1904; birth and death years not found
body: MNopedia's history of Indian immigration to Minnesota names Hira Singh as the first known Indian to move permanently to the state. He was a Sikh from Lahore, then part of India, and he enrolled at the University of Minnesota in 1904 to study mining engineering. He was the first Indian enrolled there. The essay's chronology, though, calls Mohan Singh Sekhon, who came in 1931, the first Indian American to settle in Minnesota.

That is about all the record we found says. A 1905 Minneapolis Journal article listed in MNopedia's sources is headed "Hindoo is Here to Study Mining," a reminder of how newcomers from India were described at the time.
people.connectToWork: When a community's first arrivals appear in the record as a single line, what could you do to learn more, and from whom?

sources.label: MNopedia (MNHS), "From the Ganges to Ten Thousand Lakes"

people.name: Mohan Singh Sekhon
people.dates: Arrived in Minnesota in 1931; birth and death years not found
body: In 1931, by MNopedia's account, a student named Mohan Singh Sekhon arrived on a Japanese freighter. He studied at Hamline University and later at the University of Minnesota, where he earned a degree in medicine. He stayed in the United States, and his daughter also became a doctor. The chronology in the same MNopedia essay calls Sekhon the first Indian American to settle in Minnesota, while its text gives that place to Hira Singh.
Sekhon came during the years when the law described on this page in the Thind and Saund entries kept people from India from becoming citizens.
people.connectToWork: How does someone's legal status shape what they can do with the training they have, and how would you find that out without making status the first question you ask?

sources.label: MNopedia (MNHS), "From the Ganges to Ten Thousand Lakes"

people.name: Padmakar K. Dixit
people.dates: Birth and death years not found
body: In 1958 the biochemist Padmakar K. Dixit was offered a job running the anatomy lab at the University of Minnesota. MNopedia calls him one of the earliest immigrants from India to the state.

In 1961 he officiated the first Hindu wedding in Minnesota, which, by MNopedia's account, required the Legislature to pass a special law. In 1962 the Dixits bought a house in Southeast Minneapolis, the first house in Minnesota purchased by an Indian American. It served as a refuge for Indian students when they arrived.
keyFacts: 1958: Offered a job at the University of Minnesota.
1961: Officiated the first Hindu wedding in Minnesota.
1962: Bought the first Indian American-owned house in Minnesota.
people.connectToWork: A Minnesota wedding once took a special act of the Legislature. Which of your forms or rules assume a certain kind of family, ceremony or officiant, and who has to work around them?

people.name: Mahendra Nath
body: Mahendra Nath was born in India, came to the United States in the mid-1960s, and went to college in India and in Minnesota, according to the South Asian American Digital Archive. Twin Cities Business says he arrived with $800, took a job, opened a store and reinvested what it earned. By the time he entered the Minnesota Business Hall of Fame in 2002, it says, he owned 138 fast-food restaurants, two hotels and more than 1,000 apartment units.

Normandale Community College describes Nath Companies, based in Bloomington, as a family business he built with his wife, Asha Nath, and says he helped envision and fund the Hindu Temple of Minnesota in Maple Grove. In a 1994 oral history he discussed his efforts to organize the Indian Club at the University of Minnesota.
keyFacts: Mid-1960s: Came to the United States.
1997: The Naths received the University of St. Thomas Family Business of the Year Award.
2002: Inducted into the Minnesota Business Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: A family business and a volunteer club can both become part of a community's support system. Which of these do you know about in your area, and what would you do before asking them to help?

people.name: Gopal Khanna
body: In 2005 Governor Tim Pawlenty appointed Gopal Khanna as Minnesota's first chief information officer, a Cabinet-level post leading the new Office of Enterprise Technology. He stayed until December 15, 2010, and oversaw statewide technology planning and budgets.

Government Technology says he earned degrees in economics, mathematics and political science in his native India and an MBA in the United States, and worked in business before joining the George W. Bush administration. There he became chief information officer and chief financial officer of the Peace Corps. He later led a health and human services data project for the State of Illinois, and in May 2017 he was named director of the federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.
keyFacts: 2002–2005: Senior posts in the George W. Bush administration, including at the Peace Corps.
2005–2010: Minnesota's first chief information officer.
2017: Named director of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.
people.connectToWork: State data systems decide what can be seen about the people a program serves. Who decided what your system records about language, ethnicity and disability, and what can't it show?

people.name: Amit Sood
body: MNopedia names Dr. Amit Sood of the Mayo Clinic among Minnesota's Indian American physicians known nationally and internationally. His current program's site says he was a professor of medicine and chair for student life and wellness at Mayo Clinic, and that he received Mayo awards in 2010, 2013 and 2016.

That site describes him as executive director of the Global Center for Resiliency and Wellbeing and creator of the Resilient Option program. It says he has written or co-written more than 70 peer-reviewed papers and books including The Mayo Clinic Guide to Stress-Free Living and The Mayo Clinic Handbook for Happiness.
people.connectToWork: Stress and burnout advice is often written with one kind of worker and one kind of family in mind. How would you check whether a wellness resource you offer fits the people you are offering it to?

people.name: Ashwin Madia
body: Ashwin Madia was the DFL nominee for Minnesota's 3rd Congressional District in 2008. The Minnesota Historical Election Archive records that he was born Jigar Ashwin Madia in Boston in March 1978, lived in Plymouth, and served as a U.S. Marine Corps judge advocate from 2002 to 2006.
He won the primary without opposition, with 20,830 votes, and lost the general election with 40.85 percent. The archive lists him as an attorney with his own firm, Madia Law.

2002–2006: U.S. Marine Corps judge advocate.
2008: DFL nominee for Minnesota's 3rd Congressional District.
people.connectToWork: What do you assume about a person's connection to military service, and could your intake or outreach miss a veteran because of those assumptions?

people.name: Har Gobind Khorana
body: In 1976 a laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology finished something no one had done before. It built a fully working, human-made gene that functioned inside a living cell. The team was led by H. Gobind Khorana. Eight years earlier he had shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for helping to work out the genetic code.

Khorana was born in 1922 in Raipur, a small village in Punjab, then part of British India and now in Pakistan. UPI's obituary notes that his family was poor but that his father valued education, which helped him win a scholarship to Punjab University in Lahore. He earned a bachelor's degree there in 1943 and a master's in 1945, both in chemistry and biochemistry. He earned a doctorate at the University of Liverpool in England in 1948. He then did postdoctoral work at the Federal Institute of Technology in Switzerland, where he met his wife, Esther Elizabeth Sibler. In 1952 he joined the British Columbia Research Council in Vancouver and stayed about eight years.

In 1960 he moved to the University of Wisconsin–Madison as co-director of the Institute for Enzyme Research. He became a U.S. citizen in 1966. His Wisconsin work asked how the chemical sequence of RNA tells a cell which proteins to build. In 1968 he shared the Nobel Prize with Robert Holley of Cornell and Marshall Nirenberg of the National Institutes of Health for this work.

In 1970 Khorana moved to MIT, where he became the Alfred P. Sloan Professor of Biology and Chemistry. The 1976 synthetic gene came from his lab there. He retired from the faculty in 2007 and died of natural causes in Concord, Massachusetts, on November 9, 2011, at 89.
keyFacts: 1922: Born in Raipur, Punjab, British India, now in Pakistan.
1948: Earned a Ph.D. at the University of Liverpool.
1960: Joined the University of Wisconsin–Madison.
1966: Became a U.S. citizen.
1968: Shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
1970–2007: Professor at MIT.
2011: Died in Concord, Massachusetts, on November 9.
people.connectToWork: Khorana's path crossed four countries before he reached the Midwest. How would you ask about a person's path here, rather than assuming it began with a single move from one place to another?

people.name: Jhumpa Lahiri
body: In 2000, a first book of short stories won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. Interpreter of Maladies (1999) told quiet stories about Bengali families in India and in the United States. Its author, Jhumpa Lahiri, was 32, according to the National Endowment for the Humanities. The same book also won the PEN/Hemingway Award.

Lahiri was born in London in 1967 to Indian parents from West Bengal. When she was two, the family moved to the United States after her father was offered a job as a university librarian. She grew up in Rhode Island. Bengali was the first language of her life, spoken at home; English was the language she read and wrote in outside the home. That split between languages became one of the central subjects of her writing. She earned an MFA at Boston University and then held a seven-month fellowship at the Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown, Massachusetts.

Her novel The Namesake (2003) and her story collection Unaccustomed Earth (2008) followed. Unaccustomed Earth won the Frank O'Connor International Short Story Award. Her novel The Lowland (2013) was a finalist for both the Booker Prize and the National Book Award.

Then she did something unusual for a celebrated English-language writer. She moved to Rome and began writing in Italian. In altre parole (2015), about learning a new language as an adult, appeared in English in 2016 as In Other Words. Her Italian novel Dove mi trovo (2018) appeared in her own English translation as Whereabouts (2021). She also translates the Italian novelist Domenico Starnone into English, including Ties (2016) and Trust (2021).

President Obama appointed her to the President's Committee on the Arts and the Humanities in 2010, and she received the National Humanities Medal in 2014. She directed Princeton's creative writing program for three years. As of October 2026, at Barnard College, Columbia University, she is the Millicent C. McIntosh Professor of English and directs the creative writing program.
keyFacts: 1967: Born in London.
Moved to the U.S. at age two and grew up in Rhode Island in a Bengali-speaking home.
1999: Published Interpreter of Maladies.
2000: Won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the PEN/Hemingway Award.
2013: The Lowland was a Booker Prize and National Book Award finalist.
2014: Received the National Humanities Medal.
people.connectToWork: Lahiri read and wrote in one language and spoke another at home. When a form asks for someone's language, what does your answer field miss, and how would you ask what language works for what purpose?

people.name: Vijay Iyer
body: As a small boy in upstate New York, Vijay Iyer was learning violin, which he began at age three. His sister took piano lessons, and around age four or five he started "messing on it and figuring things out little by little," he told an interviewer. That largely self-taught pianist grew up to be one of the most honored jazz musicians in the United States.

Iyer was born in Albany, New York, in 1971, the son of immigrants from Tamil Nadu, India. His father, a scientist, and his mother came in the mid-1960s, part of a wave of technically trained immigrants who arrived after a change in U.S. immigration law. He earned a B.S. from Yale College in 1992 and then went to the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned a master's in physics and, in 1998, an interdisciplinary Ph.D. in the cognitive science of music.

He took violin lessons until he was 18, stopping in his sophomore year of college when physics left no time. He built a career as a pianist, composer and bandleader in New York. His album Historicity topped the 2009 Village Voice Jazz Critics' Poll. He has studied Carnatic music, the classical tradition of South India, and draws on its mathematically structured rhythms in his compositions. His official site says his work is documented on thirty albums, several on the ECM label. He has worked with trumpeter Wadada Leo Smith and singer Arooj Aftab and has written for the Silk Road Ensemble and the Brentano String Quartet.

In 2013 he received a MacArthur Fellowship. DownBeat named him Pianist of the Year in 2014 and Artist of the Year in 2015. In January 2014 he joined Harvard University as the Franklin D. and Florence Rosenblatt Professor of the Arts. As of October 2026 his site lists a joint appointment between the Department of Music and the Department of African and African American Studies.
keyFacts: 1971: Born in Albany, New York.
1992: B.S. from Yale College.
1998: Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley.
2009: Historicity topped the Village Voice Jazz Critics' Poll.
2013: MacArthur Fellowship.
2014: Became the Rosenblatt Professor of the Arts at Harvard.
people.connectToWork: Iyer studied physics and made his career in music. When you hear a story about what families from a background expect of their children, how would you check it against the person you are actually working with?

people.name: Mindy Kaling
body: In August 2002, a recent college graduate took an off-Broadway stage in New York dressed as Ben Affleck. The play was Matt & Ben, a comedy she co-wrote with her friend Brenda Withers about how Affleck and Matt Damon came to write Good Will Hunting. The performer was Mindy Kaling, and the show helped launch her television career.

Kaling was born Vera Mindy Chokalingam on June 24, 1979, in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Her father, Avu Chokalingam, is a Tamil architect from Chennai. Her mother, Swati Chokalingam (née Roy-Sircar), was a Bengali obstetrician-gynecologist from Mumbai; the two met while working in Nigeria. Tamil and Bengali come from the south and east of India, so her family joined two regional cultures. She graduated from Dartmouth College in 2001 with a degree in playwriting.

She joined the writing staff of NBC's The Office and also played Kelly Kapoor on the series, which ran from 2005 to 2013. In 2012 she created The Mindy Project, which she wrote, produced and starred in as Dr. Mindy Lahiri, an obstetrician-gynecologist like her mother. It ran until 2017.

With Lang Fisher she co-created Never Have I Ever (2020–2023), a Netflix comedy centered on a South Asian American teenage girl, Devi Vishwakumar, and her family. Kaling has also written books of essays, including Is Everyone Hanging Out Without Me? (And Other Concerns) (2011) and Why Not Me? (2015).

The National Endowment for the Arts awarded her the 2021 National Medal of Arts "for giving voice to a new generation of storytellers." She received it from President Joe Biden at the White House on March 21, 2023.
keyFacts: 1979: Born in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
2001: Graduated from Dartmouth College.
2002: Co-wrote and starred in Matt & Ben off-Broadway.
2005–2013: Writer and actor on The Office.
2012–2017: Created and starred in The Mindy Project.
2020–2023: Co-created Never Have I Ever. Received the 2021 National Medal of Arts in 2023.
people.connectToWork: Kaling's parents came from two different regions and languages of India. Before you match someone with an interpreter or a resource because they are Indian, what would you ask first?

people.name: Nikki Haley
body: On January 24, 2017, the U.S. Senate voted 96–4 to confirm the governor of South Carolina as ambassador to the United Nations. Nikki Haley, daughter of Sikh immigrants from Punjab, became the first Indian American to serve at Cabinet level in a U.S. administration. She represented the United States at the UN until the end of 2018.

She was born Nimrata Nikki Randhawa on January 20, 1972, in Bamberg, South Carolina. Her parents came from Amritsar, Punjab. Her father, Ajit Singh Randhawa, was a biology professor at Voorhees College, and her mother, Raj Kaur Randhawa, opened a gift shop that grew into the clothing business Exotica International. Beginning at age 13, Haley kept the business's books. She earned a degree in accounting from Clemson University in 1994 and joined the family firm that year. In an interview with MidlandsBiz, she called herself its acting chief financial officer.

In 2004 she won a seat in the South Carolina House of Representatives, becoming the first Indian American to hold office in the state, according to Biography.com. She was reelected in 2006 and 2008. In 2010 she was elected governor and was reelected in 2014. She was South Carolina's first woman governor and the second U.S. governor of Indian descent, after Bobby Jindal of Louisiana.

President-elect Donald Trump chose her for the UN post on November 22, 2016. She announced her resignation on October 9, 2018, effective at year's end. In February 2023 she launched a campaign for the Republican presidential nomination. She finished second to Trump and suspended her campaign on March 6, 2024.
keyFacts: 1972: Born in Bamberg, South Carolina, to Sikh immigrants from Punjab.
1994: Graduated from Clemson University.
2005–2011: South Carolina House of Representatives.
2011–2017: Governor of South Carolina, the state's first woman governor.
2017–2018: U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, at Cabinet rank.
2023–2024: Candidate for the Republican presidential nomination.
people.connectToWork: Public figures from one background can hold very different political views. How do you keep one well-known person from standing in for everyone you serve who shares their heritage?

people.name: Sachin Dev Pavithran
body: Sachin Pavithran was born in India and grew up in the United Arab Emirates. He lost his sight as a child. At 17 he moved to the United States to study at Utah State University, where he went on to earn bachelor's degrees in Business Information Systems and Marketing, a master's in Vocational Rehabilitation Counseling, and a PhD in Disability Disciplines focused on disability policy.

At Utah State's Center for Persons with Disabilities he became Director of Policy and Program Director of the Utah Assistive Technology Program, and he taught engineering students to design with disabled users in mind. He uses screen-reading software in his own work and has spent more than twenty years developing and testing assistive technology.

In 2012 he was appointed a public member of the U.S. Access Board, the federal agency that sets accessibility guidelines. He was reappointed in 2016, served as vice chair and chair, and helped update the Section 508 standards for federal information and communication technology. On December 8, 2020, the Board named him Executive Director, and as of October 2026 its staff page still lists him in that post. He has also been President of the national board of the Association of University Centers on Disabilities and chaired the National Federation of the Blind's Committee on Autonomous Vehicles and Innovations in Transportation.
keyFacts: Born in India, raised in the United Arab Emirates, and came to the U.S. at 17.
Lost his sight as a child.
2012: Appointed a public member of the U.S. Access Board and reappointed in 2016. Served as vice chair and chair.
2020: Named Executive Director in December.
Earned a Ph.D. in Disability Disciplines at Utah State University.
people.connectToWork: Pavithran helped write the federal rules for accessible technology and uses a screen reader himself. Who in your work tests a document or a system with the tools people actually use, and when in the process do they get to do it?

people.name: Anjali Forber-Pratt
body: Anjali Forber-Pratt was born in 1984 in Calcutta (now Kolkata), India. After about two and a half months in an orphanage she was adopted by a family in Natick, Massachusetts. About two months after she arrived, she developed transverse myelitis, a spinal cord disorder that left her paralyzed from the waist down. She was not expected to survive.

At age 5 she went to a disability sports clinic at the Massachusetts Hospital School. By 9 she was racing nationally. As a wheelchair racer she won two bronze medals at the 2008 Beijing Paralympics and represented Team USA at the 2012 London Paralympics.

She earned a B.S., an M.A. in speech-language pathology, and a PhD at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. As an assistant professor at Vanderbilt University, she researched disability identity: how disabled people come to understand and claim disability as part of who they are. She received the AAPD Paul G. Hearne Leadership Award and was named a White House Champion of Change, both in 2013, and in 2020 received the American Psychological Association's inaugural Citizen Psychologist Award for advancing disability as a human rights issue. In 2021 she was named director of the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living and Rehabilitation Research (NIDILRR), the federal government's main disability research institute.

Her former post at NIDILRR has ended. As of October 2026, the University of Illinois Chicago lists her as professor and head of its Department of Disability and Human Development. The sources we found say nothing about how she describes her own cultural identity, so this page does not either.
keyFacts: 1984: Born in Calcutta, now Kolkata, and adopted by a family in Massachusetts as an infant.
2008: Won two bronze medals as a wheelchair racer at the Beijing Paralympics, and competed again in London in 2012.
Earned a Ph.D. at the University of Illinois. Her research centers on disability identity.
2021: Named director of the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living and Rehabilitation Research.
people.connectToWork: Forber-Pratt studies how people come to understand and claim disability as part of who they are. How would you ask someone how they see their own disability, and leave room for an answer that surprises you?

institutions.name: India Association of Minnesota
institutions.type: Community and cultural organization; producer of IndiaFest
institutions.location: Twin Cities; IndiaFest is held at the State Capitol, St. Paul
body: Every August, the lawn of the Minnesota State Capitol fills with booths, a parade and a ceremony raising both the American and Indian flags. This is IndiaFest, run by the India Association of Minnesota, known as IAM.

IAM's own timeline says it was incorporated in 1973 as India Club, with a concert that raised money for drought relief in India as its first fundraiser. It joined the School of India for Languages and Culture at the Festival of Nations in 1979. Sources disagree on the early dates. IAM says the first India Day was held in St. Paul in 1983, that it moved to the Landmark Center in 1985, and that the group took its current name in 1993. MNopedia says the group was renamed in 1980 and held its first India Day at the Landmark Center in 1983, and Sahan Journal in 2024 said the festival started in 1985 at the Landmark Center. In 2009 India Day became IndiaFest and moved to the Capitol grounds.

In 1992 the group completed an oral history project with the Minnesota Historical Society, recording the experiences of Indians who arrived in the 1950s and 1960s. On September 11, 2002, it held an interfaith prayer at the Capitol to remember the 9/11 attacks.

In 2023 IndiaFest marked the association's 50th anniversary. Sahan Journal counted 106 booths, and IAM's president that year, Tanwi Prigge, said walking up to the Capitol with hundreds of people behind her "always gives me goosebumps." Sahan Journal reported in August 2024 that the festival draws up to 20,000 visitors a year. IAM describes itself as non-religious and non-political. As of October 2026 its site lists Mangala Acharya as president, and it held a community town hall on immigration policy changes in July 2026.
keyFacts: 1973: Incorporated as India Club.
1983: First India Day in St. Paul, by IAM's account (Sahan Journal dates the start to 1985).
1993: Renamed India Association of Minnesota, by IAM's account (MNopedia says 1980).
2009: IndiaFest moved to the State Capitol grounds.
2023: IAM marked its 50th anniversary at the State Capitol.
institutions.connectToWork: IndiaFest is open to the public. If you went to learn, what would you do differently from going to recruit participants for your program, and who would you ask before you did either?

institutions.name: Hindu Society of Minnesota and the Hindu Temple of Minnesota
institutions.type: Place of worship and cultural center
body: In 2006 the Hindu Temple of Minnesota opened in Maple Grove. MNopedia calls it one of the largest Hindu temples in the United States, MPR News in 2009 called it the largest in Minnesota, and CCX Media in 2021 called it one of the largest in North America. It is owned by the Hindu Society of Minnesota, which says it was founded in 1978.

Building the temple took three to four years, according to the society's chair in 2022, and artisans from India built its mini temples. CBS Minnesota counted 19 deities at the shrine in 2022; the society's site now lists 21. CBS reported that members come from India, Bhutan and Nepal, and quoted a figure of 24 languages spoken. The society runs a school (the Hindu American Temple School), a youth group, yoga, guided visits, food services and senior enrichment services.
In 2013 and 2014, the society used an $8,500 state Arts and Cultural Heritage Fund grant to record 15 oral history interviews about its history.
keyFacts: 1978: Society founded, by its own account.
2006: Maple Grove temple opened.
2013–2014: State-funded oral history project.
Offers guided temple visits.
institutions.connectToWork: A place of worship may also be where language, food and senior support happen. If someone tells you it matters to them, how would you ask whether they want it involved, and keep it private if they do not?

institutions.name: SEWA–Asian Indian Family Wellness
institutions.type: Nonprofit family wellness and social services
institutions.location: 6645 James Avenue North, Brooklyn Center, serving Minnesota
body: Raj Chaudhary moved to Minneapolis in 1968 to become a cancer researcher at the University of Minnesota. A 2022 American Immigration Council profile says newcomers kept coming to her and her husband for help with immigration, health referrals and domestic violence. In 2004 she made that help formal and founded SEWA-AIFW with volunteers. "It all started with domestic violence," she told the Council, and she was its CEO in that profile. Sewa means "to serve" in Hindi.

MNopedia describes the early work as protecting women in abusive relationships, providing health education and caring for home-bound seniors and other people in need. The organization is now a 501(c)(3) with a board of trustees and trained volunteers. Its site lists a 24/7 crisis line, free monthly health clinics, women's and men's groups, senior programs, legal support, and economic and civic programs. Its clinics run at places including the S.V. Temple in Edina, the Sikh Society's gurdwara in Bloomington and the Hindu Temple in Maple Grove.

MNopedia's 2017 essay reports that fewer than 3.4 percent of Indian Americans in Minnesota lived in poverty, against 11 percent of all Minnesotans, without giving the year of the data. Newer figures are higher: Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts poverty at 5.5 percent (give or take 2.1), and the state's Economic Status of Minnesotans chartbook counts about 3,000 of 43,500 Indian Minnesotans in poverty for 2019 to 2023. That is an average. It tells you nothing about the person in front of you, and SEWA's crisis line exists alongside it.

For disability, its main program is SAPNA. The name stands for South Asian Parents Network and Advocacy in one place on SEWA's page and South Asian Persons of Neurodiverse Abilities in another, and sapna means "dream" in Hindi. SEWA describes autism, ADHD and dyslexia as different ways of thinking, learning and communicating, and notes that neurodivergent South Asian young people may be misjudged as lazy or disobedient. SAPNA offers parent education and advocacy, social skills groups for autistic people, monthly sensory-friendly events, sibling and family groups, peer support and a podcast, SAPNA Dreamers.
keyFacts: 2004: Founded by Raj Chaudhary with volunteers.
Runs SAPNA, its neurodiversity program.
Free monthly health clinics in several Twin Cities locations.
institutions.connectToWork: An average income figure can hide people who need help. When your team hears that a group is doing well, what would you check before deciding it does not need outreach, an interpreter or a crisis contact?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Indian or Asian Indian means people with roots in India, who differ widely by religion, region, language, caste, class, generation and how long they have been in the U.S. We did not find a Minnesota study of how Indian Minnesotans understand disability, and we found no Minnesota data on their use of disability services. The research below is thin: one small U.S. interview study, one small Canadian interview study, and one physician's opinion essay.
questions: How do you and your family talk about what's going on? What words do you use for it?
Has anyone given you or your child a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who in your family helps make decisions about care? Would you like anyone else at our meetings?
I will explain who sees your information. Is there anyone you would prefer not to know about these services?
What language is most comfortable for you, and for the person receiving services?
What do you hope for your child, or for yourself, in five years? What worries you about the years ahead?
Are there religious or traditional practices that are important to you that we should plan around?
Would it help to talk with other parents who share your background, or would you rather not?

context.heading: What one U.S. study heard from parents
body: Zechella and Raval (2016) interviewed 15 Asian Indian immigrant parents in the U.S., 8 mothers and 7 fathers, whose children had Down syndrome or an autism diagnosis. Parents described their local Indian community's early struggle to accept intellectual and developmental disability, which they linked in part to religious explanations. They named family support, wider awareness and access to resources as their main supports. They also described taking things one day at a time, adjusting academic hopes, working to pass on cultural heritage, and worrying about who would care for their child later.

This is 15 people, read from the published abstract, and none are identified as Minnesotans. It gives you topics to ask about, including what happens after the parents are gone. It does not tell you what any family thinks.

sources.label: Zechella and Raval, Journal of Child and Family Studies (2016), abstract

context.heading: One physician's view on stigma and disclosure
body: In a 2026 opinion essay in STAT, child psychiatrist Ritu Goel argues that stigma is the main barrier to care for South Asian families, ahead of language, insurance or distance. She writes about izzat, or family honor, and about karma, and says mothers are often blamed. She describes a mother at her clinic who had not told anyone outside her household about her 7-year-old son's diagnosis, and who had not used the full range of services because using them meant telling people.

This is one clinician's view, not a measured finding. We found no peer-reviewed U.S. study on karma or family honor and disability among Indian Americans. Many people hold medical and religious explanations at once, and many hold neither of the ones described here.

Goel writes that a parent who minimizes symptoms may not be in denial. She calls for navigators who share a family's language and background, and for culturally specific respite and caregiver support. In your own work, explain plainly who will see a person's information. Ask before involving a temple, gurdwara, mosque or church, because privacy may matter a great deal.

sources.label: Goel, STAT First Opinion (June 15, 2026)

context.heading: A study from Ontario
body: Shafi, Karunakaran and Ahmad (2024) analyzed nine interviews with South Asian immigrant parents of autistic children in Ontario, Canada. Parents reported barriers to diagnosis and to services, and pronounced stigma around autism. The sample is small, it is not limited to people from India, and Canada's systems are not Minnesota's. It does not mention karma or family honor.

sources.label: Shafi, Karunakaran and Ahmad, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2024)

context.heading: Words and language
body: India has many languages, including Hindi, Gujarati, Tamil, Telugu, Punjabi, Bengali, Urdu and Malayalam. Ask about a specific language, not "Indian," and do not assume Hindi. Many people speak fluent English, so do not assume an interpreter is needed or not needed. Fluent English also does not mean someone knows waiver or service terms, so explain them in plain language.

Divyang, or "divine body," is a Hindi term promoted by the government of India in recent years. In the Indian Journal of Medical Ethics, Khetarpal and Singh (2016) criticize it as a cliché that implies divine powers making up for a deficiency, and they argue that accessible environments and equal opportunity matter more than new labels. Some people may use it as a polite term and others reject it. We could not find a source on other disability terms in Indian languages, so none are offered here. Ask the person and the interpreter which words they use.
SEWA-AIFW uses the language of neurodiversity for autism, ADHD and dyslexia. That is one organization's framing. A person may or may not share it.

sources.label: Khetarpal and Singh, Indian Journal of Medical Ethics (2016)
SEWA-AIFW, Neurodiversity

context.heading: Who is missing from this research
body: Most of what we found is about parents of children. We found almost nothing in the voices of Indian American disabled adults, or about caste, Muslim, Sikh, Christian or Jain families, older adults, or people on temporary work visas. Sachin Dev Pavithran and Anjali Forber-Pratt, profiled on this page, are two public leaders with disabilities and roots in India, and they speak for themselves. Forber-Pratt's research on disability identity asks how people come to understand and claim disability, which is a useful question for anyone. A Minnesota study would fill a real gap.

sources.label: University of Illinois Chicago, Anjali J. Forber-Pratt
Zechella and Raval, Journal of Child and Family Studies (2016), abstract

communityRoutes.name: SEWA-AIFW SAPNA
communityRoutes.purpose: Neurodiversity program offering parent education and advocacy, social skills groups for autistic people, monthly sensory-friendly events, and sibling and family groups. An option to offer, never a requirement.

communityRoutes.name: SEWA-AIFW crisis line and services
communityRoutes.purpose: 24/7 crisis line at 952-912-9100, plus behavioral health support, free monthly health clinics and senior programs.

organizations.intro: MNopedia's 2017 essay counts about 3,670 Indian Americans in Minnesota in 1980, 8,234 in 1990 and 33,031 in 2010. Sahan Journal reported more than 50,000 in 2023, the state's second-largest Asian group. These are population estimates that say nothing about any household. MNopedia also records groups organized by language and region, such as the Gujarati Samaj, the Telugu Association of Minnesota, Minnesota Malayalee Association, Marathi Association of Minnesota, Minnesota Punjabi Society, Odisha Society of Minnesota and Minnesota Sangeetha Kannada Koota, and faith communities such as the Sri Venkateswara Temple, the Islamic Center, Geeta Ashram and Indian Christian churches. We could not find current websites for all of them, so they are not listed individually. The university's Indian Student Association began as the Indo-American Club in the 1940s, and India Abroad, a national weekly founded in 1970, ended print in March 2020. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: Jain Center of Minnesota
entries.location: Jain temple inside the Hindu Temple of Minnesota, 10530 Troy Lane North, Maple Grove
entries.purpose: Formed in October 1989. Teaches Jain philosophy and rituals through a religious school, holds events, runs a sports club and live-streams services. It reports more than 100 families.

entries.name: Sikh Society of Minnesota
entries.location: Gurdwara at 9000 West Bloomington Freeway, Bloomington
entries.purpose: Describes itself as the only gurdwara in the state, welcoming people of all faiths, governed by an eleven-member board. Runs a school with Punjabi language study, a library and a medical clinic. In 2012 a past president told MPR he estimated 500 to 600 Sikh families in Minnesota and western Wisconsin.

entries.name: BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir
entries.location: 2300 Freeway Boulevard, Brooklyn Center, with a new mandir planned in Medina
entries.purpose: A Hindu temple in the Swaminarayan tradition, with daily worship hours and youth programs. Inaugurated in 2003. BAPS reports that it consecrated a site in Medina in 2023 for a new building of more than 46,000 square feet.

entries.name: ISKCON Minnesota
entries.location: Minneapolis, at Minnehaha Avenue and 40th Street in 2025 coverage
entries.purpose: A Hindu (Gaudiya Vaishnava) center and registered nonprofit. Holds weekday evening programs and a Sunday feast. Reported in 2025 to be looking for a permanent home, so check its site for the current location.

entries.name: School of India for Languages and Culture
entries.location: Saturdays at Como Park Senior High School, 740 Rose Avenue West, St. Paul
entries.purpose: A secular nonprofit school established in 1979, with classes on Indian languages, history, culture, festivals, food, art, dance and music.

entries.name: Bengali Association of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Says its mission is to preserve the heritage of Bengal. Holds Durga Puja (October 16 to 18 in 2026), Lokhi Pujo and other events.

entries.name: Minnesota Tamil Sangam
entries.location: Twin Cities, with school campuses in Hopkins and Woodbury
entries.purpose: A nonprofit serving Minnesota since 2003, by its own account. Its Tamil School teaches more than 350 students, and it holds events including Pongal and Sangamam.

entries.name: Indian Music Society of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Presents Hindustani and Carnatic classical concerts and lecture-demonstrations. A state Legacy grant funded six concerts and two lecture-demonstrations from April 2025 to March 2026.

entries.name: Ragamala Dance Company
entries.purpose: Dance company founded by Ranee Ramaswamy and David Whetstone in 1992, with a training center and community programs. See the profiles of Ranee and Aparna Ramaswamy on this page.

entries.name: Nritya Kalakshetra Academy of Performing Arts
entries.purpose: Teaches Bharatanatyam and other forms under Sivanuja Balaji, and has performed at IndiaFest.

entries.name: IAM Media TV and newsletter
entries.purpose: The India Association of Minnesota's channels for community events, performances, IndiaFest and civic announcements. Linked from its site.

entries.name: Sannikat
entries.purpose: The Bengali Association of Minnesota's member-written magazine, in print around Durga Puja each year. The name means nearness.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Covers Minnesota immigrant communities, including IndiaFest and Indian American residents.

entries.name: Hindu American Foundation
entries.purpose: Founded in 2003. By its own account, runs education and advocacy on behalf of Hindu Americans. It speaks for itself and not for all Hindu Americans.

entries.name: Indian American Impact
entries.purpose: Described in a 2024 PTI wire report as a Democratic think tank that runs Desis Decide, a voter mobilization summit in Washington, DC. The same report records objections from several Hindu groups to speakers at that event.

entries.name: American Association of Physicians of Indian Origin
entries.purpose: Says it is the voice of more than 16,000 physicians of Indian origin, with advocacy and community service programs.

entries.name: Sikh Coalition
entries.purpose: Founded as a volunteer group in 2001 in response to hate violence after 9/11. Offers free legal help for Sikhs facing bias, hate or discrimination, along with Know Your Rights resources.

entries.name: Indiaspora
entries.purpose: A nonprofit community of Indian diaspora leaders. Publishes reports and runs 250 at 250, a project on Indian American history.

entries.name: Federation of Indian Associations, Chicago
entries.purpose: One of several separate regional federations. No single national body was found. Its site lists a gala in August 2026.

entries.name: The American Bazaar
entries.purpose: Covers startups, business, technology, politics, immigration and community, with many stories about Indian Americans.

entries.name: India Currents
entries.purpose: A nonprofit Indian American publication covering news, commentary, culture, health and immigration.

entries.name: News India Times and Desi Talk
entries.purpose: A national weekly and regional New York and Chicago editions, from the publisher that also produces Gujarat Times.

entries.name: India Tribune
entries.purpose: Says it has served the community since 1977, and covers Midwest organizations.

entries.name: NRI Pulse
entries.purpose: Indian American news, including immigration and community stories.
